lead: Hebrews calls Jesus “the apostle and high priest of our confession” and compares him with Moses: Moses was faithful in God's house as a servant, Christ over it as a son, “and we are his house”. In the Gospel the apostle John wants to stop a man who drives out demons in Jesus' name because he is not one of their group, and Jesus says, “Do not stop him.” Both readings are about the household of God: who builds it, who belongs to it, and how wide its doors are.

r.h: Faithful as a son over God's house
set: Hebrews has just called Jesus “a merciful and faithful high priest” (2:17). Now the author takes up the word “faithful” and sets Jesus beside Moses, the greatest figure in Israel's history. The comparison is made with deep respect for Moses. It rests on Numbers 12:7, where God defends Moses against Aaron and Miriam: “he is entrusted with all my house.”
str: v. 1: consider Jesus, apostle and high priest.
v. 2: he was faithful, as Moses was.
vv. 3–4: the builder and the house; God is the builder of all things.
vv. 5–6a: Moses as a servant in the house, Christ as a son over it.
v. 6b: we are his house, if we hold firm.
kw: This is the only place in the New Testament where Jesus is called an apostle. He is the one sent from God to us, and the priest who goes from us to God.
Both a building and a household, the family who live in it. Here it means God's people.
The word used of Moses in the Greek of Numbers 12:7. It is an honourable word for a trusted attendant, not a slave.
Literally “saying everything”, the boldness of one who has the right to speak. In Hebrews it is the confidence with which Christians may come before God (4:16; 10:19).
vv: consider that Jesus, the apostle and high priest of our confession,
“Confession” is homologia, the faith that the Church says aloud together, as in the Creed.
Yet Jesus is worthy of more glory than Moses, just as the builder of a house has more honor than the house itself.
Moses belongs to the house; he is one of its greatest members. Jesus belongs on the builder's side, with God, who builds all things (v. 4).
Christ, however, was faithful over God’s house as a son, and we are his house if we hold firm the confidence and the pride that belong to hope.
A gift and a condition. We are already the house. We remain so by holding on in hope.
ch: The Church calls herself the house of God, in which his family dwells (CCC 756). The Second Vatican Council teaches that the common priesthood of the faithful and the ministerial priesthood each share, in its own way, in the one priesthood of Christ (Lumen Gentium 10). Easter week, when the early Church welcomed the newly baptized, is a fitting time to remember that we are not visitors in this house but its living stones (1 Peter 2:5).

set: This short exchange closes Jesus' ministry in Galilee in Luke's Gospel. Just before it the disciples argued about which of them was the greatest, and Jesus set a child beside him (9:46–48). In the next verse Jesus sets his face to go to Jerusalem (9:51), and John, with his brother James, will soon want to call down fire on a Samaritan village (9:54). Here John speaks for the group.
str: v. 49: John reports: we tried to stop him, because he does not follow with us.
v. 50: Jesus: do not stop him; whoever is not against you is for you.
kw: To act in someone's name is to act with his authority and power. The man was calling on Jesus, and it worked.
The tense can describe an attempt: we kept trying to stop him. The same verb appears when Jesus says of the children, “do not stop them” (18:16).
vv: we tried to stop him, because he does not follow with us.
The reason is revealing: not “he does not follow you”, but “he does not follow with us”. The disciples have mixed up loyalty to Jesus with belonging to their own circle.
Do not stop him; for whoever is not against you is for you.

Luke also records the other saying, “Whoever is not with me is against me” (11:23). The two do not contradict each other. One is about our own stand toward Christ, where there is no neutral ground; the other is about how we regard others who call on his name, where we should be generous.
ch: Moses gave the same answer when Joshua wanted to stop two men who were prophesying in the camp: “Would that all the Lord’s people were prophets” (Numbers 11:29). The Second Vatican Council teaches that many elements of sanctification and truth are found outside the visible structure of the Catholic Church, gifts that belong to the Church of Christ and impel toward unity (Lumen Gentium 8; CCC 819). This is not indifference about the truth. It is joy wherever Christ's name is honoured, and a longing for full communion.

study: “We are his house.” What does it change in my week to think of my parish not as a building I visit but as a household I belong to?
When have I been slow to rejoice at good done by Christians outside my own group or Church? What would Jesus' “Do not stop him” ask of me?
